verdicts.claim: (b) UMAP and t-SNE plots distort global structure, distances and cluster sizes (Wattenberg et al. 2016; Chari & Pachter 2023). They are useful for QC (batches, outliers, mislabeled samples), not as evidence that a reduced-dimension model will perform best.
verdicts.correction:
The core point holds, with five corrections.

(1) Wattenberg, Viegas & Johnson (Distill 2016) cover t-SNE only. Their section headings are "Cluster sizes in a t-SNE plot mean nothing," "Distances between clusters might not mean anything" and "Random noise doesn't always look random." For UMAP, cite its own documentation instead: "UMAP, like t-SNE, does not completely preserve density" and "can also create false tears in clusters."

(2) How much global structure survives depends largely on initialization. Kobak & Linderman (2021, Nat Biotechnol 39:156-157) find that UMAP's apparent advantage comes from its informative default initialization; with the same initialization, UMAP does not preserve global structure any better than t-SNE. Distances are still not preserved.

(3) Chari & Pachter go further than the consensus: they say such embeddings are "counter-productive for exploratory, biological analyses" and should be "cartoon diagrams to be displayed post-analysis." Lause, Berens & Kobak (2024, PLOS Comput Biol 20:e1012403) rebut this. They show the embeddings preserve local neighbourhoods and cluster structure, but agree that they "distort distances and should not be blindly trusted" and that "generated insights should be validated by other means." So cite both papers, not Chari & Pachter alone.

(4) QC by eye is a proposal, not a finding. Tran et al. (2020, Genome Biol 21:12): "the assessment metrics did not always agree with each other, nor did the metrics always agree with our visual inspections of t-SNE and UMAP plots." A batch or outlier seen in UMAP should be confirmed by a quantitative check in the full space (e.g., PCA scores, kNN or batch-mixing metrics). For tabular nutrition and metabolomics data, the established QC view is the PCA scores plot (Broadhurst et al. 2018).

(5) An embedding coloured by the outcome is a predictor-outcome view, not an outcome-blind one. Visible class separation in 2D neither shows nor rules out that a reduced model will predict best; only the in-fold comparison can.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Reading cluster sizes and inter-cluster distances off t-SNE or UMAP, and treating visible clusters as support for a model, is customary but unsound. The claim's restriction is sound. Calling the embeddings useless for exploration (Chari & Pachter) overstates it.

verdicts.claim: (c) Any reduction used as model input (PCA, UMAP) must be fitted inside each fold, or it leaks under prediction.
verdicts.correction:
The rule is right, but it contradicts a standard textbook qualification, so the app should cite the evidence. ESL p.246: "initial unsupervised screening steps can be done before samples are left out ... Since this filtering does not involve the class labels, it does not give the predictors an unfair advantage." Hornung et al. (2015, BMC Med Res Methodol 15:95) test this directly. For normalization done on the whole dataset before CV, they found no "noteworthy optimistic bias." For PCA done before CV, they found "medium to strong underestimates of the prediction error ... in multiple settings," and concluded that "PCA has to be performed anew in each CV split." Moscovich & Rosset (2022, JRSS-B 84:1474) show that unsupervised preprocessing before CV can bias the estimate in either direction: "By default, the various preprocessing stages should be incorporated into the cross-validation scheme."

Four corrections:

(1) Say what is actually wrong. No outcome information leaks. Test-row predictors shape the representation, which biases the resampling estimate: typically optimistic for PCA, either direction in general.

(2) Scope. Every data-dependent step goes in-fold: centring and scaling, loadings, the UMAP graph, and the number of components if it comes from the data (a rule applied per fold, or nested tuning). Fixed row-wise transforms such as log or clr have nothing fitted and need no refit.

(3) t-SNE cannot be a model input in a fold-honest pipeline, because there is no out-of-sample map. scikit-learn's TSNE has fit and fit_transform but no transform. UMAP has transform, but its documentation says this assumes train and test distributions are consistent and points to parametric UMAP when they are not.

(4) The EDA plots themselves (scree, PCA, UMAP) must be computed without the sealed holdout rows. Otherwise the human's outcome-blind decision was already shaped by holdout predictors.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Sound, but uncustomary in places. The textbook custom (ESL) treats unsupervised preprocessing before CV as safe. The empirical and theoretical evidence (Hornung 2015; Moscovich & Rosset 2022) says that is unsafe for PCA.

extra_examples: How many dietary-pattern components to keep. A PCA or factor-analysis scree on food groups is outcome-blind and may set the number of patterns, but only through a stated retention rule such as parallel analysis (Horn 1965) or MAP. The usual rule, eigenvalue > 1, is not good enough. Zwick & Velicer (Psychol Bull 1986;99:432-442, results as given in Zwick's 1983 dissertation abstract): parallel analysis and MAP were "generally the best across all situations," and "Kaiser's method tended to severely overestimate the number of components." Jannasch et al. (Br J Nutr 2018;120:601-611) found pan-European dietary-pattern studies "predominantly applied ... the eigenvalue criterion and scree plot". That makes eigenvalue > 1 customary but unsound in nutrition epidemiology. Declare whether PCA runs on the covariance or correlation matrix (Jolliffe & Cadima 2016). Under prediction, rerun the rule inside each training fold; under inference, fix it in the analysis plan before any estimate.

Relative-abundance views and compositional representation. This answers the owner's own example. A stacked relative-abundance plot (microbiome taxa, or each food's share of intake) is outcome-blind. It legitimately shows closure (each row sums to 1), heavy zero-inflation and dominance by a few features. Those findings decide the representation: log-ratio coordinates (clr or ilr) before PCA or modeling, plus a zero-handling rule and a prevalence-filter rule. They do not decide which features to select for the outcome. Aitchison (Biometrika 1983;70:57-65): compositions show "marked curvature so that linear techniques such as standard principal component analysis are likely to prove inadequate." Gloor et al. (Front Microbiol 2017;8:2224): compositional data "exhibit spurious correlation upon subsetting or aggregation"; they recommend the clr transform and the compositional PCA biplot. clr is row-wise, so it needs no in-fold refit. Zero replacement and prevalence filters use other rows, so they do.

Metabolomics QC and feature filtering. A PCA scores plot of pooled-QC injections against study samples is outcome-blind. It can legitimately trigger drift or batch correction and feature removal by fixed thresholds. Broadhurst et al. (Metabolomics 2018;14:72): QCs should "cluster tightly in comparison to the total variance"; the QC-RSD acceptance criterion is "typically set to < 20% ... or < 30%," and the D-ratio should be "at most, < 50%." These thresholds can remove up to about 40% of features. A further filter by overall variance or intensity also cuts the dimension before testing. Bourgon, Gentleman & Huber (PNAS 2010;107:9546-51) found that filtering by overall variance before a t-test "increased the number of discoveries by 50%." They also warn that some filter/test pairs "lead to loss of type I error control," so the filter must be independent of the test statistic under the null. Under prediction, a variance filter computed on study rows is a learned step and goes in-fold (Moscovich & Rosset 2022 studied exactly this bias). QC-RSD is computed only on the QC injections and uses no outcome.

verdicts.claim: (a) Filtering features by abundance, prevalence or detection rate is outcome-blind and does not bias downstream tests or predictions, provided the filter statistic is independent of the test statistic under the null (Bourgon, Gentleman & Huber 2010). Picking the features that look different between outcome groups in that plot is supervised selection. Under prediction it must sit inside each fold (Ambroise & McLachlan 2002; ESL §7.10.2), and under inference it is not allowed.
verdicts.correction:
The core holds, but five parts need correcting.

(1) Bourgon et al. prove a narrower result than the claim states. They show the guarantee only for specific filter/test pairs: the overall mean or overall variance with the two-sample t-test on normal data, and any permutation-invariant filter with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test when samples are exchangeable. They name a combination that breaks: an overall-variance filter feeding limma's moderated t, because the filter distorts the empirical-Bayes variance prior and makes p-values too optimistic. They also warn that filtering can change the correlation among the surviving p-values, which can undermine Benjamini-Hochberg even when marginal independence holds. Nutrition analyses usually adjust for covariates (age, sex, BMI, energy, as in MaAsLin-style regressions). The paper does not cover those designs, so independence there is assumed, not proven; check it by permutation or simulation.

(2) An outcome-blind filter statistic does not make the threshold outcome-blind. DESeq2-style 'greedy' independent filtering picks the threshold that maximizes the number of discoveries. Ignatiadis et al. 2016 show this fails to keep FDR control when all hypotheses are true or power is low. Setting the cutoff by looking at an outcome-coloured plot is outcome-aware in the same way. So the threshold must be fixed in the plan, or tuned by a resampled rule.

(3) Common filters of the form 'present in ≥X% of samples in at least one group' look like prevalence filters but are not outcome-blind. Examples are the metabolomics 'modified 80% rule' and microbiome per-group prevalence filters. Bourgon et al. single out this filter ('fraction of present calls ... in at least one condition') as one that gives the conditional null heavier tails.

(4) Bourgon et al. say nothing about prediction. ESL p.246 does allow label-blind screening before CV. Moscovich & Rosset (JRSS-B 2022), however, show that unsupervised filtering before CV can bias the CV estimate in either direction, sometimes substantially, so 'does not bias predictions' is too strong (see claim c).

(5) 'Not allowed under inference' is too absolute. Picking by eye before the plan lock is circular and should be barred. But a pre-specified algorithm that selects on predictor–outcome association can still give valid inference when the inference accounts for the selection: post-double-selection lasso (Belloni, Chernozhukov & Hansen 2014), simultaneous post-selection inference (Berk et al. 2013), or sample splitting. That matches the framework's own principle: 'a proposal becomes a decision only through a rule the app can repeat and test.'

Also check an exchangeability precondition. In sequencing data, detection rate depends on library size. Weiss et al. 2017 show that proportion-based tests lose FDR control when average library size differs about 10x between groups. Before trusting a detection-rate filter and test, check library size against outcome group. That is a design-balance check, not feature selection.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Customary and sound: an overall-prevalence or mean-abundance filter with a fixed threshold, followed by a rank or permutation test. Customary but not guaranteed: DESeq2's default rejection-maximizing threshold, a variance filter before limma, and marginal filters before covariate-adjusted models. Customary but unsound for inference: per-group prevalence filters such as the modified 80% rule. Sound but uncustomary in nutrition: valid outcome-driven selection under inference through post-double-selection or sample splitting, which the claim currently forbids.

verdicts.claim: (b) Relative abundances are compositional. The closure constraint creates spurious correlations, so a relative-abundance plot should lead to a log-ratio representation (CLR, ALR or ILR; Aitchison 1986; Gloor et al. 2017) rather than analyzing proportions directly. Check how zeros are handled and when CLR is appropriate for prediction.
verdicts.correction:
The diagnosis holds. Closure gives proportions a negative correlation bias, and correlations among parts are unreliable (Gloor et al. 2017). So a log-ratio representation is the sound default for correlations or networks among parts, distance-based ordination, and linear or GLM models whose coefficients will be interpreted. 'Should lead to a log-ratio representation rather than proportions' is too strong as a universal rule, especially for prediction.

(1) Prediction evidence. Yerke et al. (Microbiome 2024) found relative-abundance transforms beat ALR, CLR and ILR/PhILR 'by a small but reliably statistically significant margin' across seven classifiers. Garach Vélez et al. (GigaScience 2025) found CLR helps logistic regression and SVM, random forest does well on relative abundances, and presence–absence performs about as well. So CLR suits linear, kernel and distance-based learners; for tree ensembles it is an option to test in resampling, not a requirement.

(2) Log-ratios are not the only sound representation. Greenacre et al. (Stat Sci 2023) argue that isometric log-ratios 'are not a prerequisite for good practice' and that power transforms need no zero replacement. Li, Li & Chen (Biometrics 2023) model proportions directly because log-ratios are 'inadequate or inappropriate' with many zeros.

(3) Zeros. CLR requires replacing zeros. A pseudocount is ad hoc and results can depend on its size (Kaul et al. 2017). Kaul et al. also distinguish structural zeros (truly absent, often only in one group) from sampling zeros (below depth); only sampling zeros should be imputed. Fix the replacement rule (pseudocount value, multiplicative replacement such as zCompositions, or ALDEx2's probabilistic approach) in the plan and add a sensitivity check. A replacement that uses column-wise information across samples is a learned step, so fit it in-fold.

(4) CLR mechanics for prediction. With a fixed pseudocount and a fixed feature set, CLR is a row-wise transform with no learned parameters, so it causes no fold leakage. Its geometric mean depends on which features are kept, so run the prevalence filter first in the same fold and apply the identical feature set to new rows. CLR columns sum to zero, which makes the design singular for an unpenalized linear model with an intercept. Use penalization, a zero-sum log-contrast model (Lin et al. 2014), or ALR/ILR.

(5) The relative plot should also raise the question of absolute load. Relative profiles 'cannot provide information about the extent or directionality of changes in taxa abundance' (Vandeputte et al. 2017). If microbial load or spike-ins are measured, quantitative profiles avoid closure altogether.

(6) For nutrition, dietary macronutrient shares are compositional too (Leite 2016/2021). There, the choice among ALR, CLR and pivot ILR is a reparametrization driven by the estimand and interpretation, not by performance.

Customary but not shown necessary: CLR before tree ensembles, where proportions match or beat it. Customary but unsound: a pseudocount of 1 chosen without a sensitivity check, and CLR fed to an unpenalized GLM with an intercept. Sound but uncustomary: power or chiPower transforms and relative-shift regression on raw proportions, and absolute (quantitative) profiling when load can be measured.

verdicts.claim: (c) Does a prevalence or abundance threshold computed on all training rows, rather than per fold, leak enough to matter for prediction?
verdicts.correction:
Short answer: usually a little, sometimes a lot, and the direction cannot be known in advance. So refit per fold by default, and never let the sealed holdout enter the computation.

The evidence:
- ESL p.246 says label-blind screening before CV gives 'no unfair advantage'.
- Hornung et al. (2015) measured the effect empirically on microarray data. Variance filtering and imputation done before CV produced 'negligible' bias, while PCA before CV produced 'medium to strong' optimism. Their variance-filtering results were preliminary.
- Moscovich & Rosset (JRSS-B 2022) proved the opposite of 'safe'. Unsupervised preprocessing before CV, including variance-based feature selection and grouping rare categories, 'can, in fact, introduce a substantial bias into cross-validation estimates and potentially hurt model selection'. The bias 'may be either positive or negative'. It vanishes as n grows with p fixed, but grows without bound as p grows with n fixed.

A prevalence threshold most resembles their rare-category case. There the sign of the bias flipped with the noise level and the validation-set size, and the bias disappeared once few categories sat near the cutoff (n/C large). In practice the leak scales with how many features have prevalence close to the threshold, which is common for sparse microbiome or untargeted metabolomics features with small nutrition-study samples.

Three practical consequences:
(1) If the holdout rows are excluded from the threshold, the final holdout estimate stays honest. The whole-training-set threshold distorts only the CV estimates used for tuning and model selection.
(2) Refitting per fold costs almost nothing. The Moscovich & Rosset fix is to treat preprocessing as 'an inseparable part of the learning algorithm'. Do the same for any data-driven zero replacement and for the CLR feature set, which depends on the filter.
(3) The app can measure the leak instead of arguing about it. Compute both variants and report Hornung's CVIIM (relative difference in CV error) or the per-fold overlap of retained features.

A prevalence computed within outcome classes is supervised. It is not covered by any of this and must go inside the fold.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Customary: filtering once on the whole dataset before CV. Moscovich & Rosset found 7 of 20 Science CV papers did some unsupervised preprocessing on the entire data, three of them by filtering categorical features on counts. It is often harmless but not guaranteed sound. Sound but uncustomary in nutrition and microbiome workflows: refitting the filter in each fold (sklearn Pipeline, caret preProcess) and quantifying the difference with CVIIM.

extra_examples: Pooled-QC precision filter in untargeted metabolomics. View: a QC-only view of feature RSD, detection rate and the D-ratio, plus a PCA of pooled-QC versus study samples coloured by run order. Decision: drop features with QC RSD above 20% (LC-MS) or 30% (GC-MS), a D-ratio above 50%, or QC detection below 70%, and correct drift when the QC points do not cluster tightly. Leakage: RSD comes from QC injections, not study rows, so it cannot leak into folds; the D-ratio uses study-sample variance, so it is a learned step to fit in-fold. Source: Broadhurst D, et al. Guidelines and considerations for the use of system suitability and quality control samples in mass spectrometry assays applied in untargeted clinical metabolomic studies. Missingness-pattern view in metabolomics or clinical labs. View: proportion missing per feature against mean intensity; missingness that piles up at low intensity points to values below the detection limit, i.e. left-censored, missing not at random (MNAR). Decision: the imputation rule. Use a censoring-aware method (QRILC or half-minimum) for left-censored features and random forest for features missing at random (MCAR/MAR); imputation is learned, so fit it in-fold. The original 80% rule (keep a feature if non-zero in ≥80% of all samples) is outcome-blind. Its common 'modified 80% rule' (≥80% in any one class) uses the outcome, which is the per-condition filter Bourgon et al. flag as not independent, so it is barred under inference and must sit in-fold under prediction. Sources: Wei R, et al. Missing value imputation approach for mass spectrometry-based metabolomics data. Spike-at-zero intake distribution from repeated 24-h recalls. View: the histogram of daily intake for a food, which shows many non-consumption days plus a skewed positive part, together with the within- versus between-person spread across repeat recalls. Decision: the representation. Model usual intake with a two-part model (probability of consuming on a given day, plus consumption-day amount, with person-level random effects), as in the NCI method. Do not log-transform with an added constant or treat a single recall as usual intake. Fitting a usual-intake model is a learned step (in-fold under prediction; pre-specified under inference). verdicts.claim: (a) A Poincaré plot (x_t against x_t+1; SD1, SD2; Brennan, Palaniswami & Kamen 2001) is a standard HRV tool and is used for CGM glucose variability. Per-person variability summaries from a person's own series (SD1, SD2, CV, MAGE) are deterministic, row-local engineered features that need no outcome and no other rows, so they can be computed before the seal. Does this hold when the series is the outcome, or overlaps the outcome window?
verdicts.correction:
It holds only when the series is a predictor or exposure whose window ends before the outcome is measured. It fails when the series is the outcome or overlaps the outcome window. There are seven corrections.
(1) Brennan 2001 criticises these measures rather than endorsing them. Its abstract says the ellipse-fitting methods 'are all measuring linear aspects of the intervals which existing HRV indexes already specify.' SD1 is approximately RMSSD/sqrt(2) (Ciccone et al. 2017: 'RMSSD and SD1 are identical metrics'). For CGM, Crenier 2014 found that 'SD1 ... was equivalent to continuous overlapping net glycemic action (CONGA)' and that SD2 'correlated with the SD of glucose levels (r >= 0.98)'. So a Poincaré view mostly proposes features the time-domain set already contains. Offering SD1 next to RMSSD or CONGA, or SD2 next to SD, adds duplicates that are almost perfectly correlated.
(2) Poincaré plots are used for CGM (Crenier 2014; García Maset 2016) but they are not standard there. The consensus says 'CV should be considered the primary measure of variability', with SD as a secondary measure (Danne 2017). The 2019 clinical core list includes %CV but not SD1, SD2 or MAGE (Battelino 2019).
(3) A metric is deterministic only once its algorithm is pinned. Fernandes 2022 reports that MAGE software 'programs have shown varying degrees of agreement', with median errors against manual calculation of 20%, 78%, 11% and 42% for four tools, and the result depends on the moving-average windows alpha and beta. SD1 also depends on the sampling interval (5 vs 15 min) and on how gaps are handled, so values from different devices are not interchangeable (Luijken 2019 shows the cost of predictor measurement heterogeneity). The rule must pin the algorithm version, lag, gap rule and data-sufficiency rule. Battelino 2019 recommends '70% of data from 14 days' and notes that correlations are 'weaker for hypoglycemia and glycemic variability'.
(4) Computing these features before the split is safe because nothing is learned across rows. This is the ESL qualification: 'initial unsupervised screening steps can be done before samples are left out' (Hastie et al. 2009, p.246). Moscovich & Rosset 2022 show that this qualification fails for unsupervised steps that learn from the data, such as rescaling, variance filters or grouping rare categories. It does not fail for row-local deterministic maps like these.
(5) If the series is the outcome, these summaries define the outcome; they are not features. Examples are a diet trial with glycemic variability or time in range as its endpoint, or variability as a mediator. Looking at the summaries is then an outcome view. Choosing among CV, SD1 and MAGE after looking is a choice among multiple endpoints, so the metric and algorithm must be fixed at the plan lock.
(6) If the feature window overlaps or follows the outcome window, the feature is partly a function of the outcome. Examples are hypoglycemia, or the postprandial response, inside the same wear period. Kapoor & Narayanan 2023 call these L2 leakage ('a feature is a proxy for the outcome variable') and L3.1 temporal leakage ('the model is built using data "from the future"'). Crenier's SFE–hypoglycemia correlation came from the same recordings, so it is descriptive and not predictive. The rule: the feature window ends at the index time, and the outcome window starts after it.
(7) Computing features row by row does not make the rows independent. When there are several windows per person, or windows overlap, resampling must group by person and block in time. Kapoor & Narayanan's L3.2: 'Nonindependence between training and test samples constitutes leakage'. Roberts et al. 2017 show that ignoring such structure leads to 'serious underestimation of predictive error'.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Poincaré plots for HRV are customary and sound as a description, but SD1 and SD2 are linear statistics that duplicate RMSSD and SDNN, so presenting them as extra nonlinear information is customary but unsound. For CGM, Poincaré metrics are sound but uncustomary; the consensus uses CV and SD. Using MAGE as a fixed feature without pinning the algorithm is customary but unsound. Computing row-local summaries before the split is sound. Computing CGM features over the same period as the glycemic outcome is unsound for prediction (leakage) however often it is done.

verdicts.claim: (b) Plotting day-1 against day-2 24-hour recall shows within-person variation. Its ratio to the between-person variance gives the attenuation factor, which motivates regression calibration or the NCI usual-intake method (Beaton 1979; Rosner, Willett & Spiegelman 1989; Tooze 2006; Kipnis). So this view legitimately informs a measurement-error decision, outcome-blind.
verdicts.correction:
It holds as an outcome-blind decision about measurement error under the inference purpose. There are six corrections.
(1) The within-to-between variance ratio is not itself the attenuation factor. Under the classical model, lambda = var(X)/(var(X)+var(U)) (STRATOS measurement-error guidance, Part 1). With k recalls averaged, lambda = s2_b/(s2_b + s2_w/k). When the model adjusts for covariates Z, the relevant lambda is conditional on Z: 'lambda = alpha_X|Z var(X|Z)/(alpha^2_X|Z var(X|Z)+var(U))'. That value is smaller than the marginal lambda a bivariate day-1/day-2 plot shows, so the plot understates attenuation in an adjusted model.
(2) Repeated 24-hour recalls are not a valid replicates study. STRATOS: 'The measurement error model for self-reported dietary intakes has been shown not to conform to the classical model, so replicates studies are not a true option. However, many investigators, in the absence of anything better, have adopted the assumption that 24-hour recalls provide unbiased measurements ... (e.g., Beaton et al.)'. The OPEN biomarker study (Kipnis 2003): 'Using the 24HR as a reference instrument can seriously underestimate true attenuation (up to 60% for energy-adjusted protein).' A person-specific bias that repeats across days looks like between-person signal in the scatter, so this view cannot reveal it. Only recovery biomarkers can.
(3) The spread off the diagonal is not pure error. Tooze 2006 says within-person variability 'consists of day-to-day variation in intake and random reporting errors'. Day 2 is also systematically lower: 'the reduction in mean levels of intake that can occur with repeat 24HRs, the time-in-sample effect'. That shift is modelled with a sequence indicator and a weekend covariate.
(4) The citations need tightening. Rosner, Willett & Spiegelman 1989 'require a separate validation study to estimate the regression coefficient lambda relating the surrogate measure to true exposure'. Tooze 2006 estimates usual-intake distributions. Regression calibration for diet–outcome models with the NCI method is Kipnis 2009, where usual intake is 'predicted as the conditional mean intake given 24HR-reported intake and other covariates in the health model'. So the calibration model never uses the outcome data, but it must carry the adjustment set fixed at the plan lock. STRATOS allows covariates Z# 'in addition to the covariates Z originally planned to be in the model for Y'. It is a learned two-stage step, and its standard errors must be bootstrapped across both stages.
(5) The purpose matters. Under prediction this view does not motivate correction. Carroll et al. 2006, §2.6: 'Generally, there is no need for the modeling of measurement error to play a role in the prediction problem ... W is error-free as a measurement of itself!' Substituting E(X|W) into the outcome model 'turns out to be equivalent to simply ignoring the measurement error'. The exception is transporting the model to a setting with a different error variance, where lambda 'may differ between populations'. Luijken 2019: 'homogeneity of measurement strategies across settings is of paramount importance in prediction research.' The legitimate prediction-side decisions are: use the mean of the available recalls as the feature, record each row's number of recalls (its error variance differs), and keep the deployment protocol fixed.
(6) The decision to correct follows from the study design: a short-term instrument is standing in for usual intake. The view measures how large the problem is; it does not decide whether to correct. If intake is the outcome, this is an outcome view, and the concern becomes differential error in Y (STRATOS).
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Using repeated recalls to estimate within- and between-person variance and attenuation is customary (the Beaton tradition; the NCI method). Treating those repeats as classical replicates is partly unsound, because it understates attenuation (OPEN; STRATOS). The outcome-blind status is sound. Regression calibration inside a pure prediction pipeline is neither customary nor generally needed (Carroll §2.6); it is warranted only for transport across measurement settings.

NCHS Vital Health Stat 2(178), 2018, used 'one-part AMOUNT-only models ... as less than 1% of the population had no reported consumption over the 2 days of recall', and a two-part model for fruit ('roughly 25% of respondents did not report fruit consumption on both days'). It fell back to the uncorrelated two-part model after 'convergence failures'. The same view, comparing day-2 means and weekend shares, motivates sequence and weekend covariates: 'sequence effects, weekend/weekday effects, and seasonality ... may be incorporated as covariates' (Tooze 2020). Two replicate views decide the scale (log or Box-Cox) on which the classical error model holds, before regression calibration: a plot of each person's within-person SD against their mean, and a Q-Q plot of within-person differences. Carroll et al. 2006, §1.7: 'Plot the sample standard deviation of the W-values for an individual against her/his sample mean ... If there are no obvious trends, this suggests that the measurement error variance does not depend on X'; then 'form a q-q plot of these differences across individuals'. The NCI method estimates the Box-Cox parameter inside the likelihood so that intake 'is transformed to normality conditionally on the covariates in the model' (Tooze 2006). That makes it a learned step: refit inside each fold under prediction, bootstrap under inference. The same applies to replicate biomarkers such as repeated urinary sodium or protein. verdicts.claim: (a) Outcome-blind properties legitimately cue the inductive bias: p >> n or strong collinearity -> penalized models; heavy tails and outliers -> robust losses or trees; zero-inflation -> hurdle or two-part models; repeated measures -> mixed models or GEE; compositional predictors -> log-ratio models.
verdicts.correction:
The principle holds, but the list has five problems.

(1) Two of the five cues are not outcome-blind. A robust loss answers heavy tails in the errors of Y. ESL 10.6 says squared-error loss "severely degrades for long-tailed error distributions and especially for grossly mis-measured y-values ('outliers')". Hurdle and zero-inflated models describe zeros in Y. Both are outcome views, and the right test is conditional on X, which needs a fitted model. A raw histogram of Y is not enough. Warton's group (Popovic, Eco-Stats blog), after simulating plain Poisson counts with a covariate-dependent mean: "If I look at the raw counts in isolation, using a histogram, or by applying a test of zero inflation, we would conclude the data is zero inflated, and we would be wrong." Warton (2005), "Many zeros does not mean zero inflation", makes the same point.
The outcome-blind versions of these two cues are different:
- Heavy tails or outliers in predictors call for a monotone transform (Heinze et al. 2024 use a pseudo-log) or for trees. ESL Table 10.1 rates trees good on "Robustness to outliers in input space" and "Insensitive to monotone transformations of inputs".
- A spike at zero in a predictor calls for an indicator plus a model of the positive part, or a two-part exposure-measurement model.

(2) Under inference, changing the loss changes the estimand. ESL 10.6: "The population solutions are f(x)=E(Y|x) for squared-error loss, and f(x)=median(Y|x) for absolute loss; for symmetric error distributions these are the same." So a robust loss is a decision about the estimand, fixed at the plan lock. Data shape alone cannot choose it.

(3) For prediction, "p >> n -> penalize" is sound. ESL 18.1: "simple, highly regularized approaches often become the methods of choice." Collinearity alone is a weaker cue. Harrell (RMS 4.6) says it "Does not affect predictions on new data if ... New data have same type of collinearities". Leeuwenberg et al. found "no effect of collinearity was observed on predictive outcomes" but unstable predictor selection, "in particular methods that perform strong predictor selection (e.g., Lasso)".
Under inference, naive penalized or selected models give invalid intervals. Belloni, Chernozhukov & Hansen (2014): "standard post-model selection estimators fail to provide uniform inference even in simple cases". The fix is post-double-selection or debiased ML, with the exposure left unpenalized. Collinearity between the exposure and a confounder is a question for the causal diagram, not for a penalty. Schisterman et al. (2017): "For models properly specified, total effect estimates remained unbiased even when there was almost perfect correlation between the exposure and a given intermediate, confounder, or collider."

(4) Repeated measures and compositionality come from the study design and the measurement process, not from exploration. Gloor et al. say microbiome data are compositional "because they have an arbitrary total imposed by the instrument."
- Mixed model versus GEE is a choice of estimand (subject-specific versus population-averaged), not something to read off a plot (Hubbard et al. 2010).
- Under prediction, clustering requires grouped or blocked CV. Roberts et al. (2017) recommend blocking "even if no correlation structure is visible in the fitted model residuals" (wording from the abstract as indexed; I could not retrieve the abstract directly to confirm it).
- Log-contrast models (Lin et al. 2014) need zero handling first. Gloor: the geometric mean "cannot be determined for sparse data without deleting, replacing or estimating the 0 count values."
- Under inference, log-ratio and leave-one-out substitution parametrizations answer different questions. Arnold et al. (2020): "researchers should explicitly consider and declare which causal effect is sought". Roosdorp et al. (2026): "each estimate represents a distinct research question."

(5) The framework's rule that learned outcome-blind steps are refitted in each fold is better supported than ESL 7.10.2's exception ("initial unsupervised screening steps can be done before samples are left out"). Moscovich & Rosset (JRSS-B 2022) show that "unsupervised preprocessing can, in fact, introduce a substantial bias into cross-validation estimates."

verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Customary, and sound for the cues that really are outcome-blind: dimension, collinearity, outliers or skew in predictors, design-based clustering and compositional measurement. Calling zero-inflation from a raw histogram of Y is customary but unsound. Picking a robust loss for a declared estimand on data shape alone is customary but unsound under inference. Refitting outcome-blind preprocessing in each fold is sound but uncommon; ESL itself makes an exception for it.

verdicts.claim: (b) Under prediction, choosing the model family by looking at predictor-outcome plots, then reporting the cross-validated score of that family, is optimistic. The honest version compares the candidate families with nested cross-validation, or a correction such as BBC-CV (Varma & Simon 2006; Cawley & Talbot 2010; Tsamardinos et al. 2018), and EDA only proposes the candidates.
verdicts.correction:
The core claim holds and the citations are accurate.
- Varma & Simon (BMC Bioinformatics 7:91, 2006): "using CV to compute an error estimate for a classifier that has itself been tuned using CV gives a significantly biased estimate of the true error ... all steps of the algorithm, including classifier parameter tuning, be repeated in each CV loop."
- Cawley & Talbot (JMLR 11:2079-2107, 2010): the effects are "often of comparable magnitude to differences in performance between learning algorithms".
- Tsamardinos, Greasidou & Borboudakis (Machine Learning 107:1895-1922, 2018): "the cross-validated performance of the best configuration is optimistically biased."
- ESL 7.10.2 gives the extreme case: predictors screened on all samples gave a CV error of 3% when the true error was 50%.

The weak point is that nested CV and BBC-CV correct only for selection that runs inside the resampling. Cawley & Talbot: model selection "must be treated as an integral part of the model fitting process and performed afresh every time a model is fitted to a new sample of data." BBC-CV bootstraps "the out-of-sample predictions of each configuration". A family the analyst rejected by eye has no such predictions. If the candidate list was proposed from predictor-outcome plots of all the data, the future outer test folds have already shaped that list. Nested CV then inherits an optimism that is usually smaller but has no bound.

The framework should state three things:
- Predictor-outcome views are drawn only on the development portion, never on the sealed holdout. The holdout, opened once, stays the honest number.
- Exploration may add candidates to a declared default family list but may not prune it.
- Every proposal is recorded as a configuration that the resampling runs.

Also, nested CV estimates the performance of the whole selection procedure, not of the single family it ends up choosing. The report should label the number that way.

A minor point: Cawley & Talbot mainly study over-fitting the selection criterion for hyperparameters. Family choice is the same mechanism, so the citation still fits.

verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Picking a family by eye and then reporting its plain CV score is customary but unsound. Nested CV or BBC-CV over a declared candidate list is sound but less common, because nested CV needs on the order of K^2 x C fits (Tsamardinos). The framework's line, that exploration only proposes candidates, is sound only if exploration never sees the holdout and never prunes the candidate list.

verdicts.claim: (c) Under inference, a functional form (for example, a spline for the exposure) should be prespecified or chosen by a rule declared before the estimate. Picking the form from exposure-outcome scatterplots is a forking path (Gelman & Loken 2013; Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies).
verdicts.correction:
The diagnosis holds and both citations support it.
- Gelman & Loken list "transformations" among the analysis choices phi that should be preregistered. Their case 3 is "a different test would have been performed given different data; thus T(y; phi(y))".
- Harrell, RMS 4.1: "Can't always use graphs or other devices to choose transformation. If select from among many transformations, results biased." RMS 4.3 counts "examining tables or graphs that utilize Y to tell you how to model variables" as spent degrees of freedom. RMS 2.4.1 adds that when choices are "not blinded to the response variable ... ordinary inferential methods are completely invalid."
- Grambsch & O'Brien (Stat Med 1991) put a number on it: with a preliminary non-linearity test before quadratic regression, "the type I error will be increased by roughly 50 per cent."

The correction is that "a rule declared before the estimate" is not enough on its own. Grambsch & O'Brien's procedure is itself a fixed, declared rule, and it still inflates type I error. Declaring the rule makes phi(.) explicit and repeatable, which ends the forking. It does not make naive confidence intervals valid. Two remedies work:
- (i) Prespecify a flexible form and keep it. Harrell places knots at fixed quantiles, says "Don't remove individual insignificant effects", and "Make certain that tests of nonlinearity are not revealed as this would bias the analyst."
- (ii) Carry the rule into the uncertainty. STRATOS TG2 (Sauerbrei et al. 2020) recommends a bootstrap "where in each bootstrap replication, the selection procedure is repeated". Grambsch & O'Brien's alpha correction also works.

Two counterweights the framework should absorb:
- STRATOS TG2: "Pre-specifying all aspects of a model is almost invariably unrealistic in observational studies. The gain of preventing bias by avoiding data-dependent model building is offset by the high cost of ignoring models which may fit the data much better than the pre-specified one." So declared data-driven rules, such as MFP or AIC over the number of knots (RMS 2.4.6), are legitimate if their uncertainty is propagated.
- Harrell's own strategy (RMS 4.1) lets the analyst "choose no. of parameters to devote to it using a general association index with Y". That is a predictor-outcome view used through a rule that hides the shape. It is stricter than eyeballing but looser than the framework's flat ban before the plan lock.

The same logic covers the forms of confounders. Flexible confounder terms or debiased ML avoid that choice.

In nutrition the customary practice is the hazard. Desquilbet & Mariotti (2010) present splines as a way "to visually and/or statistically check the assumption of linearity". Using that check to simplify the model back to linear is exactly the Grambsch-O'Brien problem.

verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Choosing an exposure's form from scatterplots, or simplifying a spline after a linearity check, is customary in nutrition but unsound. Prespecifying a restricted cubic spline with quantile knots, never simplified, is sound and becoming more common. A declared data-driven rule is sound only when its uncertainty is propagated, for example by a bootstrap that repeats the selection. That is uncommon in practice.

extra_examples: Spike at zero in a dietary exposure (alcohol, supplement use, episodically consumed foods): the exposure's histogram shows a mass at zero beside a continuous positive part. Code a binary exposed/unexposed indicator plus a function of the positive part rather than one transformed variable. Lorenz et al. (2017): "such situations can be analyzed by adding a binary indicator (exposed/nonexposed) to the regression model". Becher et al. (2012) name smoking, breastfeeding duration and alcohol as examples. Heinze et al. (2024) found spikes "which cannot be removed by any transformation". For 24-hour-recall exposures, the zero share also chooses the measurement model by a declared rule. NCHS: "If more than 5% of the analytic population reports zero intake ... that dietary component would be considered episodically consumed". Episodic components get the two-part NCI model (Tooze et al. 2006), and NCHS notes it is "not appropriate to try to select the best-fitting model based on ... AIC". This view is outcome-blind. Sources: Lorenz E, Jenkner C, Sauerbrei W, Becher H, Am J Epidemiol 2017;185:650-660 (doi:10.1093/aje/kww122); Becher H et al., Biom J 2012;54:686-700; Heinze G et al., BMC Med Res Methodol 2024;24:178 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11308558/); NCHS Vital Health Stat Series 2 No. 178 (https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/series/sr_02/sr02_178.pdf); Tooze JA et al., J Am Diet Assoc 2006;106:1575-1587.

How many spline knots, and where, and whether a flexible form is supportable at all, comes from the exposure's marginal distribution alone. Harrell: "Place knots where data exist - fixed quantiles of predictor's marginal distribution", with k=3 for n<30 and k=5 for n>=100. Heinze et al. (2024): "High-resolution histograms may help in such decisions" about "whether the functional form of a continuous predictor can be modelled flexibly, which would require a sufficient number of observations in the area where a nonlinear association with the outcome is expected", and "one may want to adjust default knot positions in case of very skewed distributions." Under prediction the quantile knots are learned, so compute them inside each fold. Under inference, fix them at the plan lock. Sources: Harrell FE, RMS sec. 2.4.6 (https://hbiostat.org/rmsc/genreg); Heinze G et al. 2024 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11308558/).

A correlation heatmap, variable-clustering dendrogram or PCA scree of intercorrelated nutrients, foods or metabolites cues data reduction that never looks at the outcome: dietary patterns from PCA or factor analysis (Hu 2002), or cluster scores and redundancy analysis. Harrell: "Data reduction is completely masked to Y, which is precisely why it does not distort estimates, standard errors, P-values, or confidence limits". Heinze et al. (2024) cut 51 predictors to 37 this way "without having to expect reduced predictive accuracy". This is the legitimate version of 'PCA makes me think fewer dimensions would do better', with two limits. First, the scree shows where the variance in X lies, not where the outcome's signal lies. Jolliffe (1982): low-eigenvalue components "can be as important as those with large variance". So the number of components is a candidate for the resampling under prediction, or a prespecified choice under inference. The loadings are learned, so refit them inside each fold (Moscovich & Rosset 2022). Second, a 2-D UMAP is a weak basis for this decision. Chari & Pachter (2023): "extreme dimension reduction ... inevitably induces significant distortion". Sources: Hu FB, Curr Opin Lipidol 2002;13:3-9; Harrell FE, RMS sec. 4.7 (https://hbiostat.org/rmsc/multivar); Heinze G et al. 2024; Jolliffe IT, JRSS-C 1982;31:300-303 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jorssc/v31y1982i3p300-303.html); Moscovich A, Rosset S, JRSS-B 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08974); Chari T, Pachter L, PLoS Comput Biol 2023;19:e1011288.

verdicts.claim: (a) STRATOS TG3's initial data analysis (IDA) framework (Huebner et al. 2018, 2020) separates IDA (data properties, quality, structure, whether the plan is feasible) from the research question, and says IDA should not look at relationships that answer it. What it allows: univariate outcome distributions, exposure distributions, positivity and overlap.
verdicts.correction:
THE CORE RULE IS CONFIRMED. Heinze et al. 2024 (TG3): "a key principle of IDA is that it should –without good reason- not anticipate analysis directly related to the research question, implying that associations between outcome and predictors are not explored, neither numerically nor graphically." Baillie et al. 2022, Rule 5: "a key IDA principle is not to touch the research question." Huebner 2020: IDA does "not touch the research questions." On feasibility, Huebner 2020 says IDA gives "insights into the suitability of a data set for a future research study", and Heinze 2024 says it serves "to confirm the appropriateness of or to refine a chosen model building strategy."

WHAT IT ALLOWS:
(1) Univariate outcome: yes, explicitly. Heinze 2024: "We included the outcome variable in univariate evaluations, but intentionally excluded it from any bivariate or multivariate analysis." Their optional outcome-blinded IDA data set permutes the outcome against the predictors, which keeps the outcome's marginal distribution. Huebner 2020's reporting review counts "Description of outcome variable(s)" and "Description of transformations in outcome variables" as IDA items.
(2) Exposure distributions: yes. The exposure is just a predictor. Checklist U1/U2 covers "structural variables, predictors and outcome". V1 covers each predictor's association with the structural variables, V2 pairwise correlations, and V3 the bivariate distributions of predictors in interactions. Heinze 2024 says the guidance extends to "the estimation of an adjusted exposure-outcome association."
(3) Positivity and overlap: not named anywhere in TG3. The Heinze 2024 checklist has no positivity, overlap or propensity item. They do fall inside TG3's allowed predictor-predictor domain, since exposure x confounders involves no outcome. The real source is Rubin's outcome-free design stage. Rubin 2008 defines design as "all contemplating, collecting, organizing, and analyzing of data that takes place prior to seeing any outcome data", including "analyses of covariate data used to create matched treated-control samples", and writes "it is critical to hide all outcome data until the design phase is complete."
Two caveats on overlap. First, the responses to poor overlap change the estimand: Crump et al. 2009 discard units with propensity outside [0.1, 0.9] (their working paper is titled "Moving the Goalposts ... by Changing the Estimand"), and Petersen et al. 2012 restrict the sample or modify the intervention. So under inference an outcome-blind overlap view can legitimately change the declared estimand, but only before the plan lock, and it must be reported. Second, not every positivity diagnostic is outcome-blind: Petersen's parametric bootstrap simulates from fitted models that include the outcome.

CORRECTIONS TO THE FRAMEWORK:
(i) The rule is qualified, not absolute: "without good reason" (Heinze 2024); "as much as possible" (Lusa 2024).
(ii) STRATOS applies the rule to prediction as well. Heinze 2024: "we focus on descriptive or predictive research questions" and "In this paper we focused on a predictive research question." So TG3 does not apply the rule only to inference, and STRATOS would call the framework's prediction carve-out (predictor-outcome views proposing candidates) EDA, not IDA: "IDA should not be confused with exploratory data analysis (EDA) ... as the latter ... explicitly evaluate associations of the outcome and the predictors." That carve-out needs its own justification (honest resampling), not STRATOS's.
(iii) TG3's own practice is looser than the framework's 'outcome alone' bucket. Lusa et al. 2024 (TG3, longitudinal): "evaluating the changes of the outcome in time is part of the outcome assessment in the IDA for longitudinal data." Their worked example plots grip strength (the outcome) by age and sex and notes "the trend towards the diminishing grip strength with age and ... the rate of change seems to accelerate over age", while the research question is "the age-associated decline of hand grip strength by sex." TurboTab's stricter line is defensible, but it is stricter than the source it cites.
(iv) TG3 supports the framework's principle that a proposal becomes a decision only through a rule. Heinze 2024: "statements on how potential IDA findings may guide the decisions in adaptive analysis strategies ... should be deterministically prespecified."

NOTE: I could not retrieve the 2018 Observational Studies full text (DOI 10.1353/obs.2018.0014; it is behind a MUSE challenge). Its six steps were confirmed through Huebner 2020 and the STRATOS IDA regression book.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Customary and sound at the core. TurboTab's line allows nothing involving the outcome except its marginal. That is stricter than TG3's own practice (longitudinal outcome trajectories by time and by structural variables), so for inference it is sound but uncustomary. Checking overlap before seeing outcomes is sound and customary in the causal-design literature (Rubin, Crump), but it comes from there, not from TG3.

verdicts.claim: (b) Looking at the outcome's own marginal distribution to choose its family or link (for example log-normal versus gamma) is generally accepted before the analysis under inference. Does STRATOS or the regression-modelling literature say so, and does this ever become a forking path?
verdicts.correction:
THE LOOK IS ACCEPTED; THE USE IS NOT SOUND.
The look itself is accepted. TG3: "Information about the empirical univariate distributions of the outcome ... is important for later modeling decisions" (Heinze 2024). Ten simple rules: "skewed distributions may lead to applying a transformation."
But the regression literature says the marginal is the wrong evidence for choosing a family:
- Gelman, Hill & Vehtari (Regression and Other Stories, §11.1): "the normal distribution on the outcome refers to the regression errors, not to the raw data ... it is possible for data y to be far from normally distributed even when coming from a linear regression model." Their example has a three-level x producing three sharp modes in y.
- TG3's own example shows the same thing: grip strength was bimodal in the marginal, but "a Gaussian distribution assumption at each wave is appropriate when separated by sex" (Lusa 2024).
- Log-normal versus gamma is a question about the conditional mean-variance relationship. Health econometrics settles it with residual diagnostics from a fitted model: the kurtosis of log-scale residuals (Manning & Mullahy 2001) and the modified Park test, which regresses squared residuals on log fitted values (Jones 2010). Both are outcome-on-predictor views, which are exactly the views the plan lock withholds.

UNDER INFERENCE, THE LINK OR SCALE IS PART OF THE ESTIMAND, NOT A SHAPE FIX.
Log-transformed OLS targets a geometric-mean ratio; a log-link GLM targets a ratio of arithmetic means. Santos Silva & Tenreyro 2006: "under heteroskedasticity, the parameters of log-linearized models estimated by OLS lead to biased estimates of the true elasticities." So declare the scale or link from the estimand before the data. For the variance family, either prespecify a deterministic residual-based rule or use a pseudo-likelihood estimator with robust standard errors. Gamble et al. 2017's SAP guideline puts these in the plan: 26c "any calculation or transformation used to derive the outcome (eg ... logarithm)", 27c "methods used for assumptions to be checked", and 27d "alternative methods to be used if distributional assumptions do not hold."

YES, IT BECOMES A FORKING PATH WHEN:
(1) The choice is ad hoc. Wicherts et al. 2016 list both as researcher degrees of freedom: A3 "deciding on how to deal with violations of statistical assumptions in an ad hoc manner" ("transform the data in various ways to approach normality") and A13 "Choosing between different options of the statistical model."
(2) The choice depends on the data, even when only one analysis is run. Gelman & Loken 2013: "had the data turned out differently, they could have done other analyses that were just as reasonable."
(3) The diagnostics move from the marginal to residuals, which is what the correct tools require.
(4) A large exposure effect leaks into the marginal (the mixture modes in the ROS example), so even the 'outcome alone' view is not fully blind.
Silberzahn et al. 2018 show that, on one data set, different analytic approaches gave odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Customary but unsound as stated. Looking at the marginal is standard IDA (7 of the 25 papers in Huebner 2020's review reported transforming the outcome). Choosing the family from that look is weak evidence. The sound version: fix the scale and link from the declared estimand, choose the variance function by a prespecified rule or use robust standard errors, and disclose any IDA-driven change.

verdicts.claim: (c) Recording and disclosing every outcome view (a count and a list in the methods) is an accepted mitigation for exploration under prediction, per TRIPOD+AI, Simmons et al. 2011 and Nosek et al. 2018.
verdicts.correction:
DISCLOSURE IS ENDORSED; A COUNT AND LIST OF OUTCOME VIEWS IS NOT AN ESTABLISHED MITIGATION, AND COUNTING DOES NOT REDUCE BIAS.

WHAT EACH SOURCE ACTUALLY SAYS:
- TRIPOD+AI is the relevant prediction guideline, and it asks for nothing like a list of views. Its protection is structural:
  - 12c: "Clarify whether all model building steps (including hyperparameter tuning) was replayed during the method of internal evaluation."
  - 12a: "confirm that there has been no data leakage."
  - 9a: "If any pre-selection of predictors, before model building, was carried out, then provide details how this was done."
  - 18c: report "any notable deviations" from the protocol.
- Simmons et al. 2011 is about hypothesis testing, not prediction. Its fix is disclosure, but of specific things: list all variables collected, all conditions, results with excluded observations kept, and results without the covariate. It is not a log of views. The authors also rejected count-based corrections: "it is unclear which and how many of them contribute to any given finding."
- Gelman & Loken 2013 explain why a count of views actually seen understates the problem: the multiplicity comes from analyses that would have been run had the data differed, "even in settings where researchers perform only a single analysis."
- Nosek et al. 2018 come closest to endorsing a view log, but under preregistration (inference). For pre-existing data they ask "Who has observed the data?" and "What observations, summaries, or findings have been communicated, and to whom?", and say "An effective preregistration will account for any loss of blinding." They are clear that disclosure does not restore validity: data-dependent paths leave "P values with unknown diagnosticity." Their remedy is structural: "the dataset is split in two ... the other part is sealed until exploration is complete."

THE CORRECTED STATEMENT: under prediction, the mitigation is that every outcome view is computed only on training folds, never on the sealed holdout, and that every choice it informs is either replayed in resampling or fixed before resampling. A choice made by eye cannot be replayed, so a residual optimism remains; disclose it as such, and do not present the count as a correction.
verdicts.customary_vs_sound: Disclosing IDA- and EDA-driven changes is customary and sound (Huebner 2020: "IDA driven alterations of the analysis plan should be reported with motivation in Methods"). A count and list of outcome views is uncustomary: no guideline asks for it. Used as transparency (which data split each view touched, and whether before or after the lock), it is sound. Used as a mitigation or correction, it is unsound.

extra_examples: Relative-abundance or feature-table filtering (microbiome taxa, metabolites, food items). An outcome-blind prevalence, mean or variance view legitimately sets a filter before testing or modelling: Bourgon, Gentleman & Huber 2010 (PNAS; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2906865/) show that filtering 'by a criterion independent of the test statistic' raises power. Outcome-blind is necessary but not sufficient: 'Certain nonspecific filters, for which the filter statistic does not depend on sample class labels, can also invalidate type I error control.' Their example is an overall-variance filter followed by limma's moderated t, where 'the p-values will be overly optimistic'. Overall mean and variance filters are independent of the standard two-sample t under normality. Under prediction, the threshold is a learned step and must be refit in each fold. The log-ratio treatment itself is set by how the data are measured, not by the plot (Gloor et al. 2017, Front Microbiol, doi:10.3389/fmicb.2017.02224: such data 'should be treated as compositions at all stages of analysis'). What the view decides is zero handling: te Beest et al. 2021 (Mol Ecol Resour, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1755-0998.13391) is titled 'Log-ratio analysis of microbiome data with many zeroes is library size dependent'.

A PCA or heatmap of metabolomic or proteomic features coloured by batch, plate or run order (outcome-blind) legitimately triggers handling batch effects (Leek et al. 2010, Nat Rev Genet, https://www.nature.com/articles/nrg2825). The boundary is sharp. Nygaard, Rodland & Hovig 2016 (Biostatistics, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4679072/) show that correcting while preserving the study-group difference 'may systematically induce incorrect group differences in downstream analyses when groups are distributed between the batches in an unbalanced manner'. They advise accounting for batch in the analysis model instead. For prediction, whole-data correction cannot be used on new samples ('In prediction problems, new samples are observed one at a time'; Parker, Corrada Bravo & Leek 2014, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4179553/). The correction has to be trained on the training split. A related point for the PCA/UMAP intuition: the same view cannot show that reduced dimensionality will predict better. Jolliffe 1982 (JRSS-C 31:300-303, https://academic.oup.com/jrsssc/article/31/3/300/6985100) gives examples where low-variance components carry the predictive signal, so dimension reduction is a candidate that resampling must test.

Replicate 24-hour recalls or repeat biomarker measures (outcome-blind) legitimately set the measurement-error model for a dietary exposure. Within- and between-person variance gives the attenuation factor lambda = var(X)/(var(X)+var(U)), which drives regression calibration. The view also decides the scale on which classical error holds: 'It is often found that the classical model holds only after a transformation (e.g., logarithmic) of the variable' (Keogh, Shaw, Gustafson et al. 2020, STRATOS TG4 Part 1, Stat Med 39:2197-2231, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sim.8532, illustrated with the OPEN dietary validation study). Limit: the non-differential-error assumption that makes this valid cannot be checked from outcome-blind data. It comes from the study design and must be stated as an assumption.
